label: Special Plane Projectivities
notes: This short appendix, printed pages 628 through 633, classifies plane projective transformations by their fixed points and fixed lines rather than by a generic eight-parameter matrix. We meet the planar homology, its degenerate cousin the elation, and the conjugate rotation, and we see why these special forms keep recurring across image mosaics and plane-induced transfers.

label: Fixed Points and Eigenstructure
notes: Every plane projectivity is read through the eigenvectors of its three by three matrix. A fixed point is an eigenvector, and a fixed line is an eigenvector of the transpose. The pattern of eigenvalues, whether real and distinct, repeated, or a complex conjugate pair, names the transformation and tells us how many correspondences pin it down.

label: The Planar Homology
notes: A planar homology fixes a whole line of points, the axis, plus one extra point off it, the vertex. Two eigenvalues coincide because the axis is a repeated fixed direction; the third differs. Algebraically the matrix is the identity plus a rank-one term built from the vertex and the axis, scaled by a single characteristic ratio.

label: Homology Geometry
notes: Walk the picture: the axis is fixed pointwise, so any axis point maps to itself. Off the axis, a point and its image lie on a line through the vertex, and that line meets the axis at a fixed point. Four collinear elements give the characteristic cross-ratio that is constant along every ray through the vertex.

label: The Characteristic Cross-Ratio
notes: The third eigenvalue ratio of a homology is exactly the cross-ratio of four points on any line through the vertex: the vertex, the axis intersection, the source point, and its image. Because this ratio is the same on every such ray, it is a single invariant that fully describes the homology once axis and vertex are fixed.

label: The Elation
notes: An elation is the limiting homology whose vertex slides onto the axis. The defining incidence is that the axis line contains the vertex, written as the axis dotted with the vertex equals zero. Now all three eigenvalues coincide, the rank-one term is nilpotent, and the map acts like a projective shear that still fixes the axis pointwise.

label: The Harmonic Homology
notes: When the characteristic cross-ratio equals minus one, the homology is harmonic and becomes an involution: applying it twice returns the identity. The vertex and any point form a harmonic range with the axis crossing and the image. Harmonic homologies model planar reflective symmetry and the relation between an object and its mirror image under perspective.

label: The Conjugate Rotation
notes: A conjugate rotation is a Euclidean rotation viewed through a homography: take a rotation matrix and sandwich it between a projectivity and its inverse. Conjugation preserves eigenvalues, so the map keeps the spectrum one and a complex conjugate pair on the unit circle, encoding the rotation angle even though Euclidean shape is gone.

label: Recovering the Hidden Angle
notes: Because eigenvalues survive conjugation, the rotation angle is read directly from the complex eigenvalue pair of the conjugated matrix, regardless of the warping homography. In the lab a thirty-six degree rotation is conjugated by a generic projectivity and the angle is recovered to machine precision from the argument of the eigenvalue.

label: Why Vision Cares
notes: These forms are not curiosities. A camera rotating about its center induces a conjugate rotation between images, the backbone of panoramic mosaics. Two views of a plane related by a screw motion, or the map a world plane induces between images through the epipoles, both turn out to be homologies, so the classification predicts their fixed geometry.

label: Synthesis and Checks
notes: We close by tying each transformation to a numerical invariant the notebook asserts: axis points fixed to machine zero, corresponding points collinear with the vertex, cross-ratios agreeing across rays, the elation incidence exact, and the conjugate-rotation angle recovered. Fixed points, fixed lines, and eigenvalues are the three lenses that name any special plane projectivity.
